articles.region: North Korea, Democratic Republic of the Congo
articles.headline: OFAC Designates Individuals and Entities Supporting North Korean IT Worker Schemes and M23 in DRC
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations targeting individuals and entities involved in North Korean government-run IT worker schemes and those supporting the M23 armed group in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). This action aims to disrupt revenue generation for the DPRK's illicit weapons programs and to address destabilizing activities in Eastern Congo.

Specifically, OFAC sanctioned 10 individuals and one entity for their roles in North Korean IT worker schemes that defraud U.S. businesses. These workers reportedly use fraudulent documents and stolen identities to secure employment, with a significant portion of their earnings being funneled back to the North Korean regime.

Additionally, the designations include entities and individuals linked to the Rwandan Ministry of Defence and the Zigama Credit and Savings Society, which are accused of providing support to the M23 armed group in eastern DRC. This support allegedly includes troops, weapons, equipment, logistical assistance, and training, as well as facilitating financial transactions and gold transport from M23-controlled territories.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks Settles with OFAC for $1.5 Million Over Russia Sanctions Violations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced a $1,529,685 settlement with Extreme Networks, Inc., a North Carolina-based cloud networking solutions provider. The settlement resolves nine apparent violations of Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations.

Between September 2018 and March 2022, Extreme Networks exported networking equipment and related services from the United States to Joint Stock Company (JSC) Moskovskiy Mashinostroitelniy Zavod Avangard (MMZA), a Russian defense manufacturer. MMZA is majority-owned by JSC Concern Almaz Antey, a designated entity.

OFAC determined that these apparent violations were voluntarily self-disclosed and egregious. This action underscores the importance of thorough sanctions-related due diligence, especially when acquiring companies or assets, and maintaining vigilance regarding sanctions risks in foreign operations.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends FAQs on Blocking, Rejecting Transactions, and Filing Reports
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has amended 11 Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) related to blocking and rejecting transactions and filing reports. This update is part of OFAC's ongoing review to ensure its published guidance remains current and clear.

The amended FAQs (10, 32, 33, 34, 35, 36, 41, 42, 49, 50, and 53) address various aspects of sanctions compliance, including jurisdictions subject to U.S. sanctions, procedures for blocking accounts and funds transfers, interest requirements on blocked funds, and when to reject rather than block a transaction.

The revisions also provide clarification on notification requirements for customers when property is blocked, account openings and transactions involving blocked persons, and the timing and procedures for reporting blocked property and rejected transactions to OFAC.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Iran-Related and Russia-Related General Licenses, Removes Belarus and North Korea Designations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new Iran-related designations, alongside the removal of certain Belarus and North Korea designations. Concurrently, OFAC issued new Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses and amended Frequently Asked Questions.

The Iran-related designations are part of 'Operation Economic Outcast,' targeting a network of legal, maritime, and shipping service providers allegedly facilitating Iran's sanctions evasion and petroleum trade. This action sanctioned five individuals, four entities, and nine vessels under Executive Order 13902.

In connection with these designations, OFAC issued Iran-related General Licenses GG and HH, authorizing certain wind-down activities through November 20, 2026. Additionally, OFAC delisted Belarusian national Andrei Alekseevich Rybakov and Chinese national Lu Hezheng, along with two China-based animation studios, from the SDN List under the Belarus and North Korea sanctions programs, respectively.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Chinese Entities Under PAIPA for Intellectual Property Theft, Issues General Licenses
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA), targeting entities connected to intellectual property theft. This action is accompanied by the issuance of associated General Licenses.

Five entities connected to Chinese national Linwei Ding, founder of Shanghai Zhisuan Technology Co. Ltd. ('Zhisuan'), have been sanctioned. The State Department alleges that Zhisuan 'has knowingly engaged in, or benefited from, significant theft of trade secrets of United States persons.'

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued PAIPA General License 1, 'Transactions Authorized Pursuant to the Cyber-Related Sanctions Regulations,' and PAIPA General License 2, 'Authorizing the Wind Down of Transactions Involving Certain Entities Blocked on October 19, 2026.' These licenses aim to provide guidance for authorized transactions and wind-down activities.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License and FAQ
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and a corresponding Frequently Asked Question (FAQ). This action is part of OFAC's ongoing efforts to adjust and clarify its sanctions programs.

While specific details of the amendments were not immediately released, such updates typically aim to refine the scope of authorized activities or provide further guidance on existing restrictions concerning Venezuela.

These amendments follow a recent trend of adjustments to Venezuela-related sanctions, including a designation removal earlier in the month, indicating a dynamic approach to U.S. policy towards the country.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iran-Related and Cuba Entities, Issues New General Licenses
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new Iran-related designations and a Cuba designation, alongside the issuance of new and amended General Licenses and Frequently Asked Questions.

Sixteen individuals and ten entities were sanctioned for allegedly enabling sanctions evasion and sustaining Iran's military and proxy forces. This action is part of a broader effort to target networks helping Iran generate revenue and access the global financial system.

Additionally, Cuba's BANCO INTERNACIONAL DE COMERCIO S.A. (BICSA) was designated pursuant to Executive Order 14404 for providing services to designated Iranian entities. OFAC also issued new Russia-related general licenses authorizing certain transactions involving Lukoil retail service stations outside Russia and certain Lukoil entities in Bulgaria, as well as an Iran-related general license covering the wind-down of transactions involving International Development Bank for Investment and Finance.

articles.headline: OFAC Removes Venezuelan Politician Jorge Jesus Rodriguez Gomez from SDN List
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has removed Jorge Jesus Rodriguez Gomez from its Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List. This delisting ends the associated asset freeze and removes obstacles for U.S. persons attempting to deal with him.

Rodriguez Gomez, who serves as the President of Venezuela's National Assembly, was initially designated in 2018 alongside other members of Nicolas Maduro's inner circle. His removal comes amid Washington's latest push for diplomacy and expansion of energy investment in Venezuela.

This action also follows the removal of Venezuela from the list of countries subject to restrictions on U.S. investment under the 2025 Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security Act (COINS Act), with the Treasury Department stating that the reasons for Venezuela's inclusion no longer exist.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations. These actions target individuals and entities involved in illicit drug trafficking and global terrorism networks.

The designations include individuals linked to the Cartel del Noreste (CDN), a Mexican criminal organization, for their involvement in horse racing enterprises and expansive criminal networks. This continues a history of targeting CDN's money laundering activities through American Quarter Horse racing.

These designations aim to disrupt the financial infrastructure of these illicit networks, reinforcing the U.S. government's commitment to combating international narcotics trafficking and terrorism financing.

articles.headline: Bank of America Settles with OFAC for $11.6 Million Over Sanctions Violations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced an $11,662,930 settlement with Bank of America, N.A. This settlement resolves 475 apparent violations of OFAC sanctions programs targeting Russia, Belarus, Iran, Burma, Somalia, narcotics, and global terrorism.

The apparent violations occurred between September 2021 and April 2025, involving approximately $14.83 million in transactions. OFAC attributed these failures to deficiencies in payment screening, delayed sanctions watchlist updates, weaknesses in alert prioritization, and human errors related to accounts associated with blocked individuals.

The largest category of violations involved 403 transactions, totaling $14.34 million, routed through 35 sanctioned banks, including Russian, Belarusian, and Iranian institutions. OFAC noted that Bank of America continued processing certain payments despite identifying weaknesses in its payment-routing systems.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks, Inc. Pays $1,529,685 in OFAC Civil Penalty
body: Extreme Networks, Inc. has paid a civil penalty of $1,529,685 to the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). This settlement resolves apparent violations of OFAC sanctions regulations.

The penalty stems from Extreme Networks' export of networking equipment and related services to a blocked Russian defense manufacturer between September 2018 and March 2022. The company's apparent violations were deemed egregious but voluntarily self-disclosed.

This civil penalty was announced in conjunction with a non-prosecution agreement with the Department of Justice, where Extreme Networks agreed to pay additional criminal penalties totaling $975,721.84 for sanctions and export control offenses.

articles.headline: Bank of America, N.A. Fined $11,662,930 by OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: Bank of America, N.A. has paid a civil penalty of $11,662,930 to the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). This penalty addresses 475 apparent violations of multiple OFAC sanctions programs.

The violations, occurring between September 2021 and April 2025, involved approximately $14.83 million in transactions. These included processing payments involving blocked banks, failing to prioritize alerts for exact name- and date of birth-matches to blocked persons, and delays in updating watchlists.

This OFAC penalty was part of a larger coordinated enforcement action by the U.S. Treasury Department, which also included a $1.2 billion penalty from FinCEN and a $750 million civil money penalty from the OCC for anti-money laundering and sanctions compliance failures.

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Pays $175,015 in OFAC Civil Penalty
body: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics has paid a civil penalty of $175,015 to the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). This settlement resolves apparent violations of OFAC sanctions regulations.

The specific details of the violations leading to this penalty were not immediately available in the public record, but such penalties typically involve transactions or dealings with sanctioned entities or jurisdictions.
OFAC civil penalties are a key tool in enforcing U.S. sanctions programs and promoting compliance within the private sector.

articles.headline: Individual Pays $1,427,230 in OFAC Civil Penalty
body: An individual has paid a civil penalty of $1,427,230 to the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). This penalty addresses apparent violations of OFAC sanctions regulations.

The details surrounding the individual's identity and the specific nature of the violations were not publicly disclosed in the summary information. However, penalties against individuals often relate to direct involvement in prohibited transactions or facilitating sanctions evasion.
This enforcement action highlights OFAC's commitment to holding both corporate entities and individuals accountable for non-compliance with U.S. sanctions laws.

articles.headline: Federal Reserve Signals Continued Vigilance on Inflation Amidst Mixed Economic Data
body: The Federal Reserve continues to signal a cautious approach to monetary policy, emphasizing ongoing vigilance against inflation despite recent mixed economic indicators. While some data points suggest a cooling economy, core inflation remains a concern for policymakers.

Recent statements from Fed officials indicate that while the pace of interest rate hikes may moderate, the central bank is not yet ready to declare victory over inflation. The labor market, though showing some signs of easing, remains robust, contributing to wage pressures.

Analysts anticipate that the Fed will closely monitor upcoming inflation reports and employment figures to guide its decisions in the coming months, with the possibility of further rate adjustments if inflationary pressures persist.

articles.headline: US Imposes Sanctions on Rwanda's Ministry of Defence Over Alleged Support for M23 in Eastern DRC
body: The United States has imposed sanctions on Rwanda's Ministry of Defence and a financial institution serving its security services, Zigama Credit and Savings Society, over alleged support for the M23 armed group in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). This action follows recent US-led peace talks between the DRC and Rwanda in Germany.

Washington accuses Rwanda of backing M23 with troops, weapons, equipment, logistical support, and training, and of introducing missile and jamming systems that threaten civilian aviation. Zigama Credit and Savings Society is alleged to have facilitated payments and financial transactions benefiting M23 and transported gold from M23-controlled territories to Rwanda.

These measures mark the third US sanctions action in 2026 targeting Rwanda or Rwandan-linked entities over the conflict in eastern DRC, highlighting ongoing international concern about the destabilization of the region.

articles.headline: OCC Announces Significant Enforcement Actions Against Major Banks for BSA/AML Deficiencies
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) has released its enforcement actions for October 2026, revealing significant penalties against major financial institutions for deficiencies in their Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) compliance programs. These actions underscore the OCC's commitment to ensuring robust anti-money laundering (AML) controls within the banking sector.

American Express National Bank, Sandy, Utah, received a Cease and Desist Order and a civil money penalty of $350 million for deficiencies in its BSA compliance program, failure to timely file suspicious activity reports (SARs), and violations related to customer due diligence and customer identification programs.

Bank of America, National Association, Charlotte, North Carolina, was assessed a civil money penalty of $750 million for similar deficiencies in its BSA compliance program, failure to timely file SARs, and sending wires with inaccurate transmittor name information. The OCC also issued Orders of Prohibition against individuals for embezzling customer funds.

articles.headline: DHS Adds Three Chinese Genomics Companies to UFLPA Entity List
body: The U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS), as Chair of the Forced Labor Enforcement Task Force (FLETF), has announced the addition of three Chinese genomics companies to the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act (UFLPA) Entity List. This update is effective October 29, 2026.

The three entities added are related companies, with Shenzhen BGI Technology Co., Ltd. (BGI Group) identified as the controlling shareholder. These additions are based on criteria related to sourcing materials from the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region (XUAR) or working with the Xinjiang government to recruit, transport, transfer, harbor, or receive forced labor or members of persecuted groups out of Xinjiang.

Effective immediately, U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) will apply a rebuttable presumption that goods produced by these entities are prohibited from entering the United States. This action aims to eliminate threats to American businesses from foreign competitors' unfair practices involving forced labor.

articles.headline: Revisions to the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) revises the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing two addresses associated with Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. from the Entity List under the destination of China, People's Republic of (China). This determination follows the removal from the Entity List of Arrow China Electronics Trading Co., Ltd., and the removal of six aliases for Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. in November 2025.

articles.headline: Removal From the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing one entity from the Entity List under the destination of Turkey.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
